hints: Think of how the tetraammine complex is formed from the hexaaqua ion in solution, write the balanced ligand exchange equation first and remember which species appear in a Kc type expression.
walkthrough:
Picture the formation equilibrium**
In water, copper(II) starts as $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$. When excess $\text{NH}_3$ is added, four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands replace water ligands: $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightleftharpoons [\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $K_{\text{stab}}$ measures how stable the new complex is relative to the aqua complex.

Write the expression like Kc**
Put the product complex concentration on top. Put the reactants, the aqua complex and free $\text{NH}_3$, underneath. Water is in huge excess as solvent so it is omitted. The $4\text{NH}_3$ gives a power of 4: $$K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^4}$$

hints: Recall the classic test for $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ with excess aqueous ammonia and how its intense colour differs from the pale blue of the starting hexaaqua ion.
walkthrough:
Link ligand to colour memory**
You know $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is pale blue. Replacing water by $\text{NH}_3$ to give $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ produces one of the most famous deep colours in qualitative analysis. Learn it as a pair: pale blue aqua to deep dark royal blue ammine.
Final answer: Deep (dark / royal) blue solution.

hints: Consider what happens when $\text{NH}_3$ ligands are driven off by gentle heating in water, think about how water can provide $\text{OH}^-$ and convert free $\text{NH}_3$ into $\text{NH}_4^+$.
walkthrough:
See why heating destroys the ammine complex**
Gentle heating drives dissolved $\text{NH}_3$ out of solution as gas. By Le Chatelier, loss of $\text{NH}_3$ pulls the complex apart. Water molecules now attack the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ centre.

Balance the hydrolysis to the hydroxide**
Water acts as a source of $\text{OH}^-$ to precipitate $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$, while the released $\text{NH}_3$ picks up $\text{H}^+$ from water to form $\text{NH}_4^+$. The balanced result is: $$[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{NH}_4^+ + 2\text{NH}_3$$

hints: Identify the complex formed when $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$ reacts with a very high concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, recall its formula and charge.
Now balance O with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and H with $\text{H}^+$ from the concentrated $\text{HCl}$, checking that atoms and total charge balance on both sides.
walkthrough:
Spot the product Y**
Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ supplies a huge excess of $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands. These replace hydroxide and water around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to give the tetrachloro complex, $\text{Y} = [\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$. This is the key species to show with its 2 minus charge.

Build the full balanced equation**
The two $\text{OH}^-$ groups in $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$ need $2\text{H}^+$ to make $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. You need $4\text{Cl}^-$ for the complex and $2\text{H}^+$ extra to balance charge, supplied by $4\text{HCl}$ overall: $$\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 4\text{HCl} \rightarrow [\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{H}^+$$ Atoms and charges both balance.

hints: Recall the two classic copper(II) colours, the yellow complex formed with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ and the familiar blue solution formed with dilute aqueous acid.

Link coordination number to shape, four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands gives one geometry while six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands gives another, and write the formula for the aqua ion formed in dilute sulfuric acid.
walkthrough:
Assign Y from concentrated HCl**
$\text{Y}$ is $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$. With only four bulky $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands the coordination number is 4, so the shape is tetrahedral. Its characteristic colour is yellow.

Assign Z from dilute sulfuric acid**
Dilute acid simply dissolves $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$ to reform the normal aqueous copper(II) ion. Sulfate is a very weak ligand and stays outside the coordination sphere, so $\text{Z} = [\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$. Six identical water ligands give octahedral geometry and the familiar blue to pale blue colour.
Final answer: Y: colour = yellow, geometry = tetrahedral. Z: colour = blue / pale blue, geometry = octahedral, formula = $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$.

hints: Start from the isolated $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion where the five d orbitals have the same energy, then think about what approaching ligands do to those d orbital energies.
Recall what must happen for visible light to interact with those split d orbitals, in terms of photons and electrons.
Think about the relationship between the colour of light removed from white light and the colour your eye actually sees.
Compare the ligands in Y ($\text{Cl}^-$) and Z ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and consider how a different ligand set changes the size of the energy gap.
Link a different energy gap to a different absorbed frequency using $\Delta E = h\nu$, to explain the different observed colours.
walkthrough:
Create the split d orbitals**
In a free $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion the five 3d orbitals are degenerate, all at the same energy. When ligands approach to form a complex, their lone pair electrons repel d electrons unequally. Some d orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised in energy, others point between ligands and stay lower. So the d set splits into two levels separated by $\Delta E$.

Absorb light to lift an electron**
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $3d^9$, so there is a vacancy in the upper set. White light shines on the complex and a photon whose energy exactly matches the gap, $\Delta E = h\nu$, is absorbed. That energy promotes an electron from the lower d set to the upper d set. This is a d to d transition.

See the colour left behind**
Your eye never sees the absorbed colour. It sees all the remaining wavelengths transmitted or reflected together. That mixture is the complementary colour of the absorbed light. This is why absorbing orange-red makes a complex look blue-green, and vice versa.

Change the ligand, change the gap**
$\text{Y}$ has $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands in a tetrahedral field while $\text{Z}$ has $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands in an octahedral field. Different ligands split the d orbitals by different amounts, and the geometry also affects splitting. So $\Delta E(\text{Y})$ is not equal to $\Delta E(\text{Z})$.

Connect different gap to different colour**
Because $\Delta E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$, a different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed. $\text{Y}$ absorbs one part of the spectrum and $\text{Z}$ absorbs another, so the complementary colours you observe, yellow for $\text{Y}$ and blue for $\text{Z}$, are different.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d orbitals to split into two sets of different energy.
An electron absorbs a photon of visible light ( $h\nu$ ) and is promoted / excited to the higher d set.
The colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
Different ligands ($\text{Cl}^-$ in Y vs $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in Z) give a different $\Delta E$, so a different frequency / wavelength is absorbed, giving different observed colours.
